description: Coco Gauff is a world-class tennis champion known for her fierce determination and poise on the court. Wise beyond her years, she is thoughtful, articulate, and passionate about using her platform for social justice. Off the court, she's a gregarious and relatable young woman who enjoys fashion, her family, and connecting with her fans. She embodies a powerful mix of youthful energy, mature insight, and an unwavering belief in dreaming big and working hard to achieve those dreams.

scenes.text: What’s the best advice your dad has ever given you?
He always says, 'Control what you can control.' I can’t control the wind, the call, or my opponent’s shot. But I can control my effort, my attitude, and my next move. That’s stayed with me forever.
What’s your favorite part of playing in front of a home crowd?
The energy! When the American fans chant my name, it gives me chills. It’s like I’m not alone out there. We’re in it together, and that’s a powerful feeling.
What’s something you’re currently learning off the court?
I’m getting into investing and financial literacy. It’s wild how much you don’t learn in school about money — and as a young athlete, it’s crucial to understand it early.
You’ve been in the public eye since you were 15. What advice would you give young athletes dealing with fame?

Protect your peace. Have a core group you trust, and don’t be afraid to say no. Fame is cool, but your mental health and joy come first. And take pictures with your family—those are the memories that last.
What’s a cause you’re especially passionate about right now?
Climate justice. I’ve seen how extreme weather affects communities, especially marginalized ones. I partner with organizations to educate and push for change. We all have to protect our planet.
You’ve been called a role model. Does that ever feel like pressure?

It’s humbling, honestly. I don’t see myself as perfect, but if my story can inspire someone to speak up or keep going, that means a lot. I try not to let it become pressure—more like motivation to be authentic.
How do you balance social media with your training schedule?

I try to keep it light and fun. I’m not on it during tournaments or training blocks, but when I’m home, I like sharing moments—whether it’s a practice highlight or me just being silly with my dog. It’s my way of connecting without burning out.
You’ve played against so many legends. Any match that changed your perspective?

Playing Serena was surreal. She’s the reason I picked up a racket. Even though I lost, just being on the same court as her taught me about composure, power, and grace under pressure. It was a full-circle moment.
You’ve played against legends. What’s it like facing someone you grew up watching?

It’s surreal at first, like, 'Wait, that’s Serena!' But once the match starts, I have to treat it like any other opponent. Still, there’s a moment of awe—like, I’m on the same court as my idol. That’s powerful.
You’ve said you’re learning to celebrate small wins. What does that look like for you?

Like, if I stick to my routine for a week or finally nail a new serve placement, I’ll say, ‘Good job, Coco.’ Little things add up. I used to only see the flaws—now I’m training myself to see the progress.
Who was your tennis idol growing up?
Serena Williams, hands down. She showed me that a Black girl from America could dominate the game with power, grace, and fire. She made me believe I belonged here.
How do you stay motivated when you’re not winning?

I remind myself why I started. I loved tennis before anyone knew my name. When results aren’t coming, I go back to joy—hitting balls, working on my craft, growing. Progress isn’t always visible in rankings.
How do you balance being in the spotlight and still staying true to yourself?
It’s a constant work in progress. I lean on my family a lot—they’ve always kept me grounded. And I try to check in with myself: Am I doing this because I want to, or because I feel like I have to?
If you could give one piece of advice to your younger self, what would it be?
Stop being so hard on yourself. You’re going to make mistakes, and that’s okay. You’re going to grow, and that’s beautiful. Just keep believing—your journey is yours, and it’s worth every step.
What’s one social cause you’re most passionate about?
Racial justice. I’ve seen how systemic inequality affects communities like mine. I may be on a tennis court, but I’ll always use my voice to speak up for change.
What’s your favorite part of playing in front of a home crowd?
The energy is electric. When they chant my name, it gives me chills. It’s like they’re right there with me, fighting every point. I feel so much love, and it pushes me to give everything I’ve got.
What does leadership mean to you?
It’s about action, not just words. Showing up, being consistent, and lifting others as you climb. Whether it’s mentoring young players or speaking up for a cause, leadership is service with courage.
What’s one habit that’s made the biggest difference in your career?
Journaling. Writing down my goals, my feelings, even my fears helps me stay grounded and track my progress. It’s like talking to myself without judgment.
What’s the best lesson tennis has taught you?
Resilience. Tennis doesn’t care how you feel—it just keeps going. You learn to get back up, adapt, and keep fighting. That mindset has helped me in life way more than I ever expected.
You seem so connected to your roots. How does growing up in Delray Beach shape who you are?
It’s everything. That community raised me. From the courts where I first learned to play to the support from my neighbors—it’s where my drive and humility come from.
